Title: Glaser’s grounded theory for qualitative entrepreneurship research: Concepts, applications, methods, and cautions

Overview and scope
Qualitative entrepreneurship research increasingly uses grounded theory to move beyond descriptive narratives toward explanatory accounts of how entrepreneurs perceive, create, and act upon opportunity in context. <cite id="979b6e00-3">Grounded theory methods provide a logically consistent set of data collection and analytic procedures aimed at developing theory, and have been adopted to make qualitative strategies in entrepreneurship rigorous and accessible</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-2">Grounded theory emerged to challenge the notion that qualitative research is impressionistic, replacing it with systematic strategies for abstraction and theory generation about social processes</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-4">Within interpretive paradigms, constructivist grounded theory (CGT) builds on Glaser & Strauss’s original while emphasizing co-constructed understandings and naturalistic procedures, aligning with entrepreneurship’s situated, processual phenomena</cite>.

What Glaser’s theory offers to entrepreneurship
Glaser’s constructionist/“Glaserian” grounded theory (CGGT/CGT) centers constant comparison as the core analytic engine and emphasizes theory construction through iterative, inductive procedures. <cite id="979b6e00-1">Glaser argued that constructionist grounded theory is the pure form of grounded theory and continued to refine it through concepts like theoretical sensitivity, detailed theoretical coding families, and explicit strategies for conceptualizing data</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-2">Glaser and Strauss emphasized using GT to explicate causes, conditions, contexts, contingencies, consequences, and covariances—components of social processes—thus enabling explanatory theory development beyond description</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-0">Applied Glaserian practice cycles incident-by-incident coding to identify semantic units, evaluates patterns, conceptualizes, discovers categories and properties, and links categories into themes; crucially, stages are not linear but interlock in cyclical feedback</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-1">Glaser’s institutionalization (Grounded Theory Institute; Grounded Theory Review) and ongoing methodological clarifications further standardize CGT as a rigorous, theory-building approach</cite>.

How GT is used in entrepreneurship: core applications
Opportunity recognition and entrepreneurial cognition
Entrepreneurship research treats opportunity recognition as foundational yet ambiguous; GT provides a scaffold to unpack entrepreneurs’ meaning-making and ability formation. <cite id="2b9c48ca-2">A grounded-theory study of university student opportunity recognition shows that rigorous GT requires continual theoretical sampling, continuous comparisons and category refinement until theoretical saturation, and validity checks using the Pandit NR method; the emergent model centers “problem discovery” as the entry point of opportunity identification</cite>. <cite id="2b9c48ca-2">Problem discovery—often via experiential noticing and explanation—triggers the recognition process, aligning with Glaser’s emphasis on emergent categories from data through constant comparison</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-3">In entrepreneurship, GT methods have been used to develop a taxonomy of entrepreneurial ventures (e.g., in Zimbabwe), illustrating how theory-guided coding and synthesis integrate data-driven abstraction with structured categorization for theoretically rich typologies</cite>.

Founders’ patterns, leadership, and network dynamics
Process-oriented constructs such as leadership in collaborative networks have been theorized using grounded methods to reveal how actors distribute (non)leadership and co-constitute shared leadership over time. <cite id="2cc34730-1">An interpretive grounded study used constant comparison, theoretical sampling, and analytic induction to iteratively blend data-inspired induction with theory-informed deduction, producing process-oriented insights on (non)leadership phenomena and shared leadership development</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-1">This approach explicitly contrasts with positivist variable analysis, treating “truth” as provisional and leadership as processual; grounded theory is neither naive empiricism nor pure relativism, and it is used to advance theory through iterative category development and integration</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-0">Such grounded-theory logic underpins entrepreneurship research that seeks to build explanatory frameworks (e.g., typologies, process theories) rather than confirm pre-existing models</cite>.

SMEs, strategy, and resource-based processes
Entrepreneurship and SME research often links GT to resource-based and strategic perspectives to understand how actors perceive, select, and act on opportunities. <cite id="2b9c48ca-4">Work drawing on Alvarez & Busenitz and Davidson & Honig highlights individual-specific resources that facilitate opportunity identification and that resource access shapes entrepreneurs’ ability to detect and act on opportunities</cite>. <cite id="2b9c48ca-4">Grounded analyses in this stream integrate qualitative evidence on perceived opportunity prevalence and gendered differences with theory-building about resource mediation, showing GT’s compatibility with strategic and resource-based theorizing</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-2">Constant comparison is used to achieve reliability by cycling between categories and data, refining behavioral patterns and coping mechanisms, and then triangulating with existing theory to build integrative frameworks</cite>.

Methodological workhorses in practice
Procedures: constant comparison, theoretical sampling, and memoing
Across entrepreneurship applications, three procedures anchor Glaser’s method: (1) constant comparison to generate abstraction, (2) theoretical sampling to elaborate categories, and (3) memo-writing to integrate insights. <cite id="2cc34730-1">Constant comparison is the core principle of grounded theorizing, entailing iterative shifts between collecting and analyzing data; theoretical sampling involves deciding what data to collect next on the basis of emergent themes and concepts</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-0">In practice, incident-by-incident comparison of semantic units, pattern evaluation, conceptualization, and category merging occur in non-linear cycles, with linkages forming themes</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-3">Memo-writing sustains analytical engagement, increases abstraction, and supports category refinement; theoretical saturation is judged when additional data reveal no new properties or insights and a solid understanding is achieved</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-4">Analytic induction within coding (initial to focused to theoretical) progressively integrates data into integrative theoretical codes; constant comparisons occur at each stage, from data-to-data to category-to-concept, culminating in a grounded theory</cite>.

Sampling and saturation (and beyond): from saturation to theoretical sufficiency
Entrepreneurship studies using GT often combine practical saturation testing with Glaserian refinements. <cite id="2b9c48ca-2">Researchers test saturation via the Pandit NR method before broadening or deepening sampling, then proceed with three-level coding; emergent categories are evaluated for redundancy versus novelty until no new properties appear</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-0">Glaser’s approach treats stages as interlocking rather than linear; semantic unit identification, pattern evaluation, and conceptualization are iteratively revised, with memoing and cross-category linkages integrating new evidence</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-0">For entrepreneurship projects, this yields a convincing analysis and a structured taxonomy, accelerating theory development while maintaining alignment with Glaser’s inductive logic</cite>.

Integrating GT with entrepreneurship theory
GT in entrepreneurship does not negate theory; it builds it from the ground up. <cite id="979b6e00-3">Charmaz frames GT as a set of schemes to guide rigorous qualitative research, making strategies explicit and accessible to entrepreneurship scholars</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-1">Analytic induction blends data-inspired induction with theory-inspired deduction to support imaginative, practice-oriented theorizing about leadership processes and shared leadership</cite>. <cite id="2b9c48ca-2">Applied models (e.g., ability structures for opportunity recognition) integrate emergent categories with established constructs, aligning Glaser’s conceptualization procedures with mainstream entrepreneurship theory</cite>.

Debates, divergences, and cautions
Grounded theory in entrepreneurship is shaped by—and sometimes contested over—paradigmatic commitments. <cite id="979b6e00-1">Glaser and Strauss’s work was a response to positivism; Glaser later advanced constructionist grounded theory, emphasizing rigorous, emergent theory and critiquing distortions toward complexity</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-4">The divergence between Glaserian and Straussian/Corbinian approaches—rooted in different epistemic stances—has produced two dominant approaches while preserving core GT tenets; constructivist GT aligns with interpretive paradigms that treat multiple realities and co-construction of meaning</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-1">Entrepreneurship studies adopting interpretive GT explicitly contrast with positivist variable analysis, acknowledging provisional truth and processual phenomena</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-0">Methodologically, Glaserian practice’s cyclical, non-linear processes and emphasis on conceptualization and category linkage are central; some studies adapt these to thematic analysis without explicit theory building, underscoring the need to clarify intentions at the outset</cite>.

Practical guidance for entrepreneurship researchers using Glaser’s theory
Design and aims
- Clarify whether your goal is theory construction or theory theming. <cite id="979b6e00-0">If developing theory, commit to Glaserian cycles of conceptualization and category linkage; if not, acknowledge that even “thematic” GT requires careful constant comparison to avoid premature abstraction</cite>.
- Start with a focused question about process and meaning. <cite id="979b6e00-2">GT excels when phenomena are processual and socially constructed, fitting topics like opportunity discovery, leadership in networks, and resource-mediated action</cite>.

Sampling and data collection
- Use theoretical sampling to elaborate categories. <cite id="2cc34730-1">Decide what data to collect next based on emergent themes; alternate streams (e.g., founders vs. investors; pre-founding vs. post-founding) can accelerate theory emergence</cite>.
- Integrate mixed methods judiciously. <cite id="2cc34730-4">Literature-informed memos and selective theoretical coding can scaffold abstraction without collapsing into pure relativism</cite>.

Analysis
- Execute constant comparison rigorously. <cite id="2cc34730-4">Run comparisons at multiple levels: data-to-data, data-to-category, category-to-category, and category-to-concept; progress from initial line-by-line codes to focused and integrative categories</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-0">Use incident-by-incident coding to surface semantic units, then conceptualize patterns and link categories; memoing threads the analysis</cite>.
- Judge sufficiency with triangulation. <cite id="2b9c48ca-2">Test saturation with Pandit NR early; refine sampling and coding until no new properties emerge; cross-validate categories with additional cases</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-2">Cycl ing between categories and data enhances reliability and robustness</cite>.

Reporting and theorizing
- Make analytic moves explicit. <cite id="2cc34730-1">State how induction and deduction interplay to advance theory; show how categories are refined into integrative theoretical constructs</cite>.
- Connect to entrepreneurship theory. <cite id="2b9c48ca-2">Translate emergent constructs (e.g., problem discovery, resource mediation) into models that relate to opportunity recognition abilities and performance</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-3">Use GT-derived typologies and process accounts to build or refine frameworks (e.g., taxonomies of ventures) rather than merely describe cases</cite>.

Common pitfalls and how to avoid them
- Premature theory imposition. <cite id="2cc34730-1">Grounded theory warns against abstracting before the data demand; analytic induction and constant comparison guard against this by revisiting data as categories mature</cite>.
- Treating qualitative as descriptive. <cite id="979b6e00-2">GT’s emphasis on conceptualization and causal condition analysis prevents the “description trap,” yielding explanatory accounts of how entrepreneurs perceive and act on opportunity</cite>.
- Overlooking paradigmatic fit. <cite id="979b6e00-4">If interpretive relativism or constructivist assumptions misalign with your aims, consider analytic GT variants or triangulation with positivist measures; specify the choice and its implications</cite>.

Illustrative applications and outcomes
- Opportunity recognition among students and early-stage entrepreneurs: <cite id="2b9c48ca-2">Emergent “problem discovery” as a precursor ability, supported by experiential explanation and experimentation</cite>; <cite id="979b6e00-0">cyclical coding and memoing yielded a coherent model integrated into entrepreneurship education and practice</cite>.
- Leadership in collaborative networks: <cite id="2cc34730-1">Processual, shared leadership theorized through constant comparison and analytic induction, advancing shared leadership theory in interorganizational contexts</cite>.
- SME strategy and resources: <cite id="2b9c48ca-4">Resource access and gender shape opportunity recognition; grounded models link resource-based mechanisms to observed patterns without discarding interpretive insights</cite>.
- Founding and coping mechanisms: <cite id="2cc34730-2">Glaserian reliability checks refined behavioral patterns and coping responses, culminating in a new framework</cite>.
- Methods dissemination: <cite id="979b6e00-3">Entrepreneurship-focused methodological essays show how GT procedures expedite theory development and make qualitative research exciting and rigorous</cite>.

Relationship to other qualitative paradigms in entrepreneurship
GT complements and contrasts with phenomenology and case study strategies in entrepreneurship. <cite id="979b6e00-4">Phenomenology often targets essential structures of experience, while GT targets explanatory processes and causal conditions; CGT’s iterative comparisons and analytic induction blend interpretive depth with theory-driven integration</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-1">Case studies can be embedded with grounded coding to move from thick description to process theory, aligning with GT’s constant comparison logic</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-0">Where phenomenology emphasizes essence, GT emphasizes emergence and linkages across categories; both can coexist when triangulated to address complementary levels of analysis</cite>.

Conclusion and outlook
Glaser’s grounded theory equips entrepreneurship researchers to build process-oriented, explanatory theories of opportunity recognition, leadership, and strategic action grounded in actors’ meanings and contexts. <cite id="979b6e00-2">By systematizing conceptualization and causal analysis, GT strengthens qualitative rigor and moves research beyond description</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-1">Its constructionist lineage, with constant comparison, theoretical sensitivity, and detailed coding families, offers a robust toolkit for theorizing in dynamic entrepreneurial settings</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-1">Interpretive grounded studies in entrepreneurship demonstrate how data–theory dialogues and analytic induction can advance shared leadership theory in networks, suggesting broader applicability to team dynamics, governance, and ecosystem processes</cite>. <cite id="2b9c48ca-2">Applied models of opportunity recognition abilities underscore GT’s utility for developing actionable frameworks and typologies that integrate with mainstream entrepreneurship theory</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-4">While debates over objectivist vs. constructivist GT persist, both streams preserve core grounded principles; entrepreneurship scholars can navigate these by clarifying aims and triangulating methods to achieve theoretically rich, empirically grounded accounts</cite>.

Key takeaways for practice
- Use constant comparison to drive abstraction, memo-writing to integrate insights, and theoretical sampling to elaborate categories until saturation or theoretical sufficiency. <cite id="2cc34730-1">These procedures enable iterative data–theory development</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-4">Structure coding into initial, focused, and theoretical phases to achieve integrative categories</cite>. <cite id="2b9c48ca-2">Test saturation early and refine sampling</cite>.
- Align methods with aims: choose GT for theory construction when mechanisms and relationships are under-theorized; supplement with theory theming when consolidating established constructs.
- Report analytic moves explicitly and triangulate with literature and mixed evidence to balance interpretive depth with external coherence.

Title: A New Explanation for the Conflict Between Constructivist and Objectivist Grounded Theory
Snippet: Since Glaser and Strauss (1967) asked "What is going on here?" and coined the term "grounded theory," it has drawn much attention. Grounded theory (GT) has allowed qualitative researchers to sensitize theoretical abstraction and concepts and generate theoretical explanations about phenomena related to human behavior. Furthermore, GT moves the qualitative research tradition beyond description due to the fact that it includes a set of general principles, guidelines, strategies, and heuristic devices (Charmaz, 2014). Glaser and Strauss (1967) offered a set of strategies to develop theory rather than to deduce testable and verifiable hypotheses from extant theories. The strategies refuted the views that qualitative research is impressionistic and unsystematic, so they made qualitative research more robust. They also discarded suppositions that qualitative research should be aligned with quantitative research standards and moved the arbitrary division between theory and research. Moreover, they allowed qualitative researchers to generate their own theories. Therefore, they challenged views that theory development should belong to the elite and enabled separation between data gathering and data analysis (Charmaz, 2014). Glaser and Strauss (1967) emphasized that GT is used to explicate causes, conditions, contexts, contingencies, consequences, and covariances, which are components of social processes. As a result, GT has enabled qualitative researchers to develop and construct theories, so it has drawn remarkable attention. In addition, GT helps qualitative researchers to go beyond description by generating explanations on what is going on. Hence, it has been used by social scientists from nursing research to education. However, a conflict about what GT is, what its components are, and what its assumptions are has arisen. As a result of the conflict, objectivist grounded theory (OGT) developed by Corbin and Strauss (1990) and constructivist grounded theory (CGT) designated by Charmaz (2008;2014) were created. 

GT has its roots in Chicago School. Glaser and Strauss (1967), inventor of GT, viewed constant comparison method as core essence of GT.

Title: Entrepreneurial orientation and new venture performance in emerging markets: the mediating role of opportunity recognition
Snippet: "One of the pillars of entrepreneurship research is the concept of 'opportunity" (Harms et al. 2009). Opportunity recognition demonstrates the capability of a firm to identify a good idea and transform it into a business impression that improves value and creates revenues (Lumpkin and Lichtenstein 2005). Opportunity recognition focuses on market and customer demands as well as helps in problem-solving to make firms successful (Shrader and Hills 2015). It also contributes to a firm's performance (Cassia and Minola 2012). Meanwhile, identifying and exploiting opportunities is still poorly understood (Nambisan and Zahra 2016;Vogel 2017;Wang et al. 2013). 

For the last 3 decades, opportunity recognition has become a key topic in the field of entrepreneurship (Donbesuur et al. 2020;George et al. 2016;Yang and Meyer 2019). However, there is little agreement on the accepted definition of opportunity recognition (Hulbert et al. 2015). For instance, Bull and Willard (1993) demonstrated that "entrepreneurship" appears under conditions of: first, a task-related motivation (certain visions or social values that motivate individuals to act); second, available expertise (knowledge about the current situation); third, a personal gain expectation (e.g., economic and psychological benefits and goals); and, fourth, a supportive environment. According to the authors, these conditions impact the ability of an individual (e.g., entrepreneur) who searches for an opportunity and aims to benefit from the opportunity. For instance, Kirzner (1985) demonstrated that an entrepreneur is one who perceives profit opportunities and undertakes actions to fill the presently unsatisfied need or process inefficiencies. 

Opportunity recognition is based on experiences and entrepreneurial characteristics (Parida et al. 2016) and entrepreneurial behavior that follows (Wasdani and Mathew 2014). Firms with strong potential towards opportunity recognition are more successful over those having little opportunity recognition in the market (Ketchen et al. 2007). Title: Understanding (non)leadership phenomena in collaborative interorganizational networks and advancing shared leadership theory: an interpretive grounded theory study
Snippet: Interpretive grounded theory (Charmaz 2014;Suddaby 2006;Glaser and Strauss 1967) is usually contrasted with a positivist approach of qualitative research (cf. e.g. Gephart 2004 on the distinction between positivist and non-positivist/interpretive qualitative research). From an interpretive perspective, ''truth'' is considered as provisional, and social life as well as leadership as processual (Charmaz 2014: 17;Charmaz et al. 2018;cf. Endres and Weibler 2017: 217f.;cf. Astley 1985;Morgan and Smircich 1980). Hence, research ''seeks interpretive understanding rather than a variable analysis that produces abstract generalizations'' (Charmaz et al. 2018: 417;Suddaby 2006). Through attending to our participants' perceptions, language, and experiences, our study sheds light on their views and practices of network leadership, and provides new theoretical insights on (non)leadership phenomena in collaborative interorganizational networks and on shared leadership development. We developed our findings through analytic induction by iteratively shifting between data-inspired induction and theory-inspired deduction for imaginative practice-oriented theorizing (Suddaby 2006;Charmaz 2014). In doing so, we rely on informed grounded theory, which is neither abstract (or naive) empiricism nor pure (subjectivist) relativism. Hence, grounded theory ''is not an excuse to ignore the literature'' (Suddaby 2006: 634;Charmaz et al. 2018: 419;Charmaz 2014). In line with this understanding, we applied ''constant comparison'' and ''theoretical sampling'', which are considered core principles of grounded theorizing (Suddaby 2006;Charmaz 2014;Glaser and Strauss 1967). Constant comparison fundamentally implies an iterative cyclical research process in which the researcher shifts between collecting and analyzing data (see below for more details). Theoretical sampling means making decisions on what data to collect next on the basis of themes and concepts that emerged with theoretical relevance for the theory that is being constructed (cf. Charmaz 2014;Suddaby 2006: 634).

Snippet: Constant comparisons and memo-writing are often relied upon when analysing data in grounded theory research. Charmaz (2006) defined the constant comparative method as: 

A method of analysis that generates successively more abstract concepts and theories through inductive processes of comparing data with data, data with category, category with category, and category with concept. Comparisons then constitute each stage of analytic development (p. 187). 

At each stage of analysis, constant comparisons were made as part of the coding process. A CGTM includes two main phases of coding-initial and focused-followed by a process of theoretical coding (Charmaz, 2006). During initial coding, we thoroughly read through the transcript data line-by-line (Jones et al., 2014) and answered the questions, "What are these data a study of?" and "What do the data suggest?" (Charmaz, 2006, p. 47); answering these questions assisted in the naming of initial codes. Next, we engaged in a process of focused coding, which permitted us to develop more selective, directed and abstract codes (Charmaz, 2006). In this stage of analysis, focused codes develop into theoretically rich and integrative categories (Jones et al., 2014). 

The final theoretical codes depict potential relationships between categories of codes developed through focused coding (Charmaz, 2006). The grounded theory that emerges from the data is founded on the formation of the integrative theoretical codes (Charmaz, 2006;Jones et al., 2014). 

Lastly, analysis occurred through a process of memo-writing, ". . . the fundamental process of researcher/data engagement that results in a "grounded" theory" (Lempert, 2007, p. 245). Memos were written with an analytical, rather than a descriptive, mindset (Jones et al., 2014). As the analysis progressed, literary resources were examined so that the theoretical underpinnings of other research could aid in identifying patterns within our dataset (Lempert, 2007).

Title: Glaser’s grounded theory for qualitative entrepreneurship research: Concepts, applications, methods, and cautions

Overview and scope
Qualitative entrepreneurship research increasingly uses grounded theory to move beyond descriptive narratives toward explanatory accounts of how entrepreneurs perceive, create, and act upon opportunity in context. <cite id="979b6e00-3">Grounded theory methods provide a logically consistent set of data collection and analytic procedures aimed at developing theory, and have been adopted to make qualitative strategies in entrepreneurship rigorous and accessible</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-2">Grounded theory emerged to challenge the notion that qualitative research is impressionistic, replacing it with systematic strategies for abstraction and theory generation about social processes</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-4">Within interpretive paradigms, constructivist grounded theory (CGT) builds on Glaser & Strauss’s original while emphasizing co-constructed understandings and naturalistic procedures, aligning with entrepreneurship’s situated, processual phenomena</cite>.

What Glaser’s theory offers to entrepreneurship
Glaser’s constructionist/“Glaserian” grounded theory (CGGT/CGT) centers constant comparison as the core analytic engine and emphasizes theory construction through iterative, inductive procedures. <cite id="979b6e00-1">Glaser argued that constructionist grounded theory is the pure form of grounded theory and continued to refine it through concepts like theoretical sensitivity, detailed theoretical coding families, and explicit strategies for conceptualizing data</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-2">Glaser and Strauss emphasized using GT to explicate causes, conditions, contexts, contingencies, consequences, and covariances—components of social processes—thus enabling explanatory theory development beyond description</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-0">Applied Glaserian practice cycles incident-by-incident coding to identify semantic units, evaluates patterns, conceptualizes, discovers categories and properties, and links categories into themes; crucially, stages are not linear but interlock in cyclical feedback</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-1">Glaser’s institutionalization (Grounded Theory Institute; Grounded Theory Review) and ongoing methodological clarifications further standardize CGT as a rigorous, theory-building approach</cite>.

How GT is used in entrepreneurship: core applications
Opportunity recognition and entrepreneurial cognition
Entrepreneurship research treats opportunity recognition as foundational yet ambiguous; GT provides a scaffold to unpack entrepreneurs’ meaning-making and ability formation. <cite id="2b9c48ca-2">A grounded-theory study of university student opportunity recognition shows that rigorous GT requires continual theoretical sampling, continuous comparisons and category refinement until theoretical saturation, and validity checks using the Pandit NR method; the emergent model centers “problem discovery” as the entry point of opportunity identification</cite>. <cite id="2b9c48ca-2">Problem discovery—often via experiential noticing and explanation—triggers the recognition process, aligning with Glaser’s emphasis on emergent categories from data through constant comparison</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-3">In entrepreneurship, GT methods have been used to develop a taxonomy of entrepreneurial ventures (e.g., in Zimbabwe), illustrating how theory-guided coding and synthesis integrate data-driven abstraction with structured categorization for theoretically rich typologies</cite>.

Founders’ patterns, leadership, and network dynamics
Process-oriented constructs such as leadership in collaborative networks have been theorized using grounded methods to reveal how actors distribute (non)leadership and co-constitute shared leadership over time. <cite id="2cc34730-1">An interpretive grounded study used constant comparison, theoretical sampling, and analytic induction to iteratively blend data-inspired induction with theory-informed deduction, producing process-oriented insights on (non)leadership phenomena and shared leadership development</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-1">This approach explicitly contrasts with positivist variable analysis, treating “truth” as provisional and leadership as processual; grounded theory is neither naive empiricism nor pure relativism, and it is used to advance theory through iterative category development and integration</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-0">Such grounded-theory logic underpins entrepreneurship research that seeks to build explanatory frameworks (e.g., typologies, process theories) rather than confirm pre-existing models</cite>.

SMEs, strategy, and resource-based processes
Entrepreneurship and SME research often links GT to resource-based and strategic perspectives to understand how actors perceive, select, and act on opportunities. <cite id="2b9c48ca-4">Work drawing on Alvarez & Busenitz and Davidson & Honig highlights individual-specific resources that facilitate opportunity identification and that resource access shapes entrepreneurs’ ability to detect and act on opportunities</cite>. <cite id="2b9c48ca-4">Grounded analyses in this stream integrate qualitative evidence on perceived opportunity prevalence and gendered differences with theory-building about resource mediation, showing GT’s compatibility with strategic and resource-based theorizing</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-2">Constant comparison is used to achieve reliability by cycling between categories and data, refining behavioral patterns and coping mechanisms, and then triangulating with existing theory to build integrative frameworks</cite>.

Methodological workhorses in practice
Procedures: constant comparison, theoretical sampling, and memoing
Across entrepreneurship applications, three procedures anchor Glaser’s method: (1) constant comparison to generate abstraction, (2) theoretical sampling to elaborate categories, and (3) memo-writing to integrate insights. <cite id="2cc34730-1">Constant comparison is the core principle of grounded theorizing, entailing iterative shifts between collecting and analyzing data; theoretical sampling involves deciding what data to collect next on the basis of emergent themes and concepts</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-0">In practice, incident-by-incident comparison of semantic units, pattern evaluation, conceptualization, and category merging occur in non-linear cycles, with linkages forming themes</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-3">Memo-writing sustains analytical engagement, increases abstraction, and supports category refinement; theoretical saturation is judged when additional data reveal no new properties or insights and a solid understanding is achieved</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-4">Analytic induction within coding (initial to focused to theoretical) progressively integrates data into integrative theoretical codes; constant comparisons occur at each stage, from data-to-data to category-to-concept, culminating in a grounded theory</cite>.

Sampling and saturation (and beyond): from saturation to theoretical sufficiency
Entrepreneurship studies using GT often combine practical saturation testing with Glaserian refinements. <cite id="2b9c48ca-2">Researchers test saturation via the Pandit NR method before broadening or deepening sampling, then proceed with three-level coding; emergent categories are evaluated for redundancy versus novelty until no new properties appear</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-0">Glaser’s approach treats stages as interlocking rather than linear; semantic unit identification, pattern evaluation, and conceptualization are iteratively revised, with memoing and cross-category linkages integrating new evidence</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-0">For entrepreneurship projects, this yields a convincing analysis and a structured taxonomy, accelerating theory development while maintaining alignment with Glaser’s inductive logic</cite>.

Integrating GT with entrepreneurship theory
GT in entrepreneurship does not negate theory; it builds it from the ground up. <cite id="979b6e00-3">Charmaz frames GT as a set of schemes to guide rigorous qualitative research, making strategies explicit and accessible to entrepreneurship scholars</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-1">Analytic induction blends data-inspired induction with theory-inspired deduction to support imaginative, practice-oriented theorizing about leadership processes and shared leadership</cite>. <cite id="2b9c48ca-2">Applied models (e.g., ability structures for opportunity recognition) integrate emergent categories with established constructs, aligning Glaser’s conceptualization procedures with mainstream entrepreneurship theory</cite>.

Debates, divergences, and cautions
Grounded theory in entrepreneurship is shaped by—and sometimes contested over—paradigmatic commitments. <cite id="979b6e00-1">Glaser and Strauss’s work was a response to positivism; Glaser later advanced constructionist grounded theory, emphasizing rigorous, emergent theory and critiquing distortions toward complexity</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-4">The divergence between Glaserian and Straussian/Corbinian approaches—rooted in different epistemic stances—has produced two dominant approaches while preserving core GT tenets; constructivist GT aligns with interpretive paradigms that treat multiple realities and co-construction of meaning</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-1">Entrepreneurship studies adopting interpretive GT explicitly contrast with positivist variable analysis, acknowledging provisional truth and processual phenomena</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-0">Methodologically, Glaserian practice’s cyclical, non-linear processes and emphasis on conceptualization and category linkage are central; some studies adapt these to thematic analysis without explicit theory building, underscoring the need to clarify intentions at the outset</cite>.

Practical guidance for entrepreneurship researchers using Glaser’s theory
Design and aims
- Clarify whether your goal is theory construction or theory theming. <cite id="979b6e00-0">If developing theory, commit to Glaserian cycles of conceptualization and category linkage; if not, acknowledge that even “thematic” GT requires careful constant comparison to avoid premature abstraction</cite>.
- Start with a focused question about process and meaning. <cite id="979b6e00-2">GT excels when phenomena are processual and socially constructed, fitting topics like opportunity discovery, leadership in networks, and resource-mediated action</cite>.

Sampling and data collection
- Use theoretical sampling to elaborate categories. <cite id="2cc34730-1">Decide what data to collect next based on emergent themes; alternate streams (e.g., founders vs. investors; pre-founding vs. post-founding) can accelerate theory emergence</cite>.
- Integrate mixed methods judiciously. <cite id="2cc34730-4">Literature-informed memos and selective theoretical coding can scaffold abstraction without collapsing into pure relativism</cite>.

Analysis
- Execute constant comparison rigorously. <cite id="2cc34730-4">Run comparisons at multiple levels: data-to-data, data-to-category, category-to-category, and category-to-concept; progress from initial line-by-line codes to focused and integrative categories</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-0">Use incident-by-incident coding to surface semantic units, then conceptualize patterns and link categories; memoing threads the analysis</cite>.
- Judge sufficiency with triangulation. <cite id="2b9c48ca-2">Test saturation with Pandit NR early; refine sampling and coding until no new properties emerge; cross-validate categories with additional cases</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-2">Cycl ing between categories and data enhances reliability and robustness</cite>.

Reporting and theorizing
- Make analytic moves explicit. <cite id="2cc34730-1">State how induction and deduction interplay to advance theory; show how categories are refined into integrative theoretical constructs</cite>.
- Connect to entrepreneurship theory. <cite id="2b9c48ca-2">Translate emergent constructs (e.g., problem discovery, resource mediation) into models that relate to opportunity recognition abilities and performance</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-3">Use GT-derived typologies and process accounts to build or refine frameworks (e.g., taxonomies of ventures) rather than merely describe cases</cite>.

Common pitfalls and how to avoid them
- Premature theory imposition. <cite id="2cc34730-1">Grounded theory warns against abstracting before the data demand; analytic induction and constant comparison guard against this by revisiting data as categories mature</cite>.
- Treating qualitative as descriptive. <cite id="979b6e00-2">GT’s emphasis on conceptualization and causal condition analysis prevents the “description trap,” yielding explanatory accounts of how entrepreneurs perceive and act on opportunity</cite>.
- Overlooking paradigmatic fit. <cite id="979b6e00-4">If interpretive relativism or constructivist assumptions misalign with your aims, consider analytic GT variants or triangulation with positivist measures; specify the choice and its implications</cite>.

Illustrative applications and outcomes
- Opportunity recognition among students and early-stage entrepreneurs: <cite id="2b9c48ca-2">Emergent “problem discovery” as a precursor ability, supported by experiential explanation and experimentation</cite>; <cite id="979b6e00-0">cyclical coding and memoing yielded a coherent model integrated into entrepreneurship education and practice</cite>.
- Leadership in collaborative networks: <cite id="2cc34730-1">Processual, shared leadership theorized through constant comparison and analytic induction, advancing shared leadership theory in interorganizational contexts</cite>.
- SME strategy and resources: <cite id="2b9c48ca-4">Resource access and gender shape opportunity recognition; grounded models link resource-based mechanisms to observed patterns without discarding interpretive insights</cite>.
- Founding and coping mechanisms: <cite id="2cc34730-2">Glaserian reliability checks refined behavioral patterns and coping responses, culminating in a new framework</cite>.
- Methods dissemination: <cite id="979b6e00-3">Entrepreneurship-focused methodological essays show how GT procedures expedite theory development and make qualitative research exciting and rigorous</cite>.

Relationship to other qualitative paradigms in entrepreneurship
GT complements and contrasts with phenomenology and case study strategies in entrepreneurship. <cite id="979b6e00-4">Phenomenology often targets essential structures of experience, while GT targets explanatory processes and causal conditions; CGT’s iterative comparisons and analytic induction blend interpretive depth with theory-driven integration</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-1">Case studies can be embedded with grounded coding to move from thick description to process theory, aligning with GT’s constant comparison logic</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-0">Where phenomenology emphasizes essence, GT emphasizes emergence and linkages across categories; both can coexist when triangulated to address complementary levels of analysis</cite>.

Conclusion and outlook
Glaser’s grounded theory equips entrepreneurship researchers to build process-oriented, explanatory theories of opportunity recognition, leadership, and strategic action grounded in actors’ meanings and contexts. <cite id="979b6e00-2">By systematizing conceptualization and causal analysis, GT strengthens qualitative rigor and moves research beyond description</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-1">Its constructionist lineage, with constant comparison, theoretical sensitivity, and detailed coding families, offers a robust toolkit for theorizing in dynamic entrepreneurial settings</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-1">Interpretive grounded studies in entrepreneurship demonstrate how data–theory dialogues and analytic induction can advance shared leadership theory in networks, suggesting broader applicability to team dynamics, governance, and ecosystem processes</cite>. <cite id="2b9c48ca-2">Applied models of opportunity recognition abilities underscore GT’s utility for developing actionable frameworks and typologies that integrate with mainstream entrepreneurship theory</cite>. <cite id="979b6e00-4">While debates over objectivist vs. constructivist GT persist, both streams preserve core grounded principles; entrepreneurship scholars can navigate these by clarifying aims and triangulating methods to achieve theoretically rich, empirically grounded accounts</cite>.

Key takeaways for practice
- Use constant comparison to drive abstraction, memo-writing to integrate insights, and theoretical sampling to elaborate categories until saturation or theoretical sufficiency. <cite id="2cc34730-1">These procedures enable iterative data–theory development</cite>. <cite id="2cc34730-4">Structure coding into initial, focused, and theoretical phases to achieve integrative categories</cite>. <cite id="2b9c48ca-2">Test saturation early and refine sampling</cite>.
- Align methods with aims: choose GT for theory construction when mechanisms and relationships are under-theorized; supplement with theory theming when consolidating established constructs.
- Report analytic moves explicitly and triangulate with literature and mixed evidence to balance interpretive depth with external coherence.

Snippet: "One of the pillars of entrepreneurship research is the concept of 'opportunity" (Harms et al. 2009). Opportunity recognition demonstrates the capability of a firm to identify a good idea and transform it into a business impression that improves value and creates revenues (Lumpkin and Lichtenstein 2005). Opportunity recognition focuses on market and customer demands as well as helps in problem-solving to make firms successful (Shrader and Hills 2015). It also contributes to a firm's performance (Cassia and Minola 2012). Meanwhile, identifying and exploiting opportunities is still poorly understood (Nambisan and Zahra 2016;Vogel 2017;Wang et al. 2013). 

For the last 3 decades, opportunity recognition has become a key topic in the field of entrepreneurship (Donbesuur et al. 2020;George et al. 2016;Yang and Meyer 2019). However, there is little agreement on the accepted definition of opportunity recognition (Hulbert et al. 2015). For instance, Bull and Willard (1993) demonstrated that "entrepreneurship" appears under conditions of: first, a task-related motivation (certain visions or social values that motivate individuals to act); second, available expertise (knowledge about the current situation); third, a personal gain expectation (e.g., economic and psychological benefits and goals); and, fourth, a supportive environment. According to the authors, these conditions impact the ability of an individual (e.g., entrepreneur) who searches for an opportunity and aims to benefit from the opportunity. For instance, Kirzner (1985) demonstrated that an entrepreneur is one who perceives profit opportunities and undertakes actions to fill the presently unsatisfied need or process inefficiencies. 

Opportunity recognition is based on experiences and entrepreneurial characteristics (Parida et al. 2016) and entrepreneurial behavior that follows (Wasdani and Mathew 2014). Firms with strong potential towards opportunity recognition are more successful over those having little opportunity recognition in the market (Ketchen et al. 2007). There is a great chance of failure if SMEs cannot search or identify opportunities in a dynamic market (Sambasivan et al. 2009).

Cohen and Winn (2007) define opportunity recognition capabilities as the firm's abilities to "perceive opportunities to existing when there is a potential to redistribute resources for the betterment of some without making others worse off" (p. 32). It is a process to match emerging consumer demand and the solution to satisfy the necessity (O'Connor & Rice, 2001). Two schools of thoughts as neoclassical equilibrium theory and Austrian theory provide the premium to opportunity recognition capabilities in the entrepreneurship literature. The neoclassical equilibrium theory assumes that an individual who possesses high-risk propensity in recognising the opportunity is considered an entrepreneur (Khilstrom & Laffont, 1979). However, the neoclassical equilibrium theory overlooks the entrepreneurship framework, sources, and the existence of opportunities (Eckhardt & Shane, 2003). Notwithstanding, Austrian theorists argue that opportunities appear from the imperfect market with information asymmetry in a scattered form (Venkataraman, 1997). In a similar vein, Kirzner (1997) emphasises that the influx of knowledge in the market influences opportunity discovery, and only a few entrepreneurs are able to recognise it. Based on this notion, Wang et al. (2013) probe that the firm's opportunity recognition depends highly on the willingness and ability of the firm to discover and create the benefit of it. Entrepreneurs can pursue an opportunity at any time in any industry (Mostafiz et al., 2019d). Aforementioned, opportunities can be derived from uncertainties; however, it is also possible that opportunities appear from circumstances of the needs of new products, services, or business (i.e., knowledge) (Barringer & Ireland, 2008). Successful entrepreneurs must recognize many opportunities to develop solid entrepreneurial intentions (Hanohov and Baldacchino, 2018). In opportunity recognition, entrepreneurs search for a good idea for a specific business using several information sources. Executing these ideas into business activity (Hassan et al., 2020). Three essential factors assist the recognition of entrepreneurship opportunities. First, "engaging in active research" enables entrepreneurs to analyze the emergence and profitability of particular opportunities. The second factor includes the customers served through a particular product or service. A third factor focuses on the prior business knowledge in the industry (Dahalan et al., 2015). According to the authors, these conditions impact the ability of an individual (e.g., entrepreneur) who searches for an opportunity and aims to benefit from the opportunity. For instance, Kirzner (1985) demonstrated that an entrepreneur is one who perceives profit opportunities and undertakes actions to fill the presently unsatisfied need or process inefficiencies. 

Opportunity recognition is based on experiences and entrepreneurial characteristics (Parida et al. 2016) and entrepreneurial behavior that follows (Wasdani and Mathew 2014). Firms with strong potential towards opportunity recognition are more successful over those having little opportunity recognition in the market (Ketchen et al. 2007). Aforementioned, opportunities can be derived from uncertainties; however, it is also possible that opportunities appear from circumstances of the needs of new products, services, or business (i.e., knowledge) (Barringer & Ireland, 2008). Timmons and Spinelli (2006) emphasise market opportunities which are meant to be focused on market demand as they increase the chances of success. Therefore, three inherent characteristics of an opportunity are as follows: (a) economic value, (b) newness (i.e., in some cases incremental), and (c) desirability and feasibility (e.g., acceptability of the product/service in the market) (Baron, 2006).

Title: Understanding (non)leadership phenomena in collaborative interorganizational networks and advancing shared leadership theory: an interpretive grounded theory study
Snippet: Interpretive grounded theory (Charmaz 2014;Suddaby 2006;Glaser and Strauss 1967) is usually contrasted with a positivist approach of qualitative research (cf. e.g. Gephart 2004 on the distinction between positivist and non-positivist/interpretive qualitative research). From an interpretive perspective, ''truth'' is considered as provisional, and social life as well as leadership as processual (Charmaz 2014: 17;Charmaz et al. 2018;cf. Endres and Weibler 2017: 217f.;cf. Astley 1985;Morgan and Smircich 1980). Hence, research ''seeks interpretive understanding rather than a variable analysis that produces abstract generalizations'' (Charmaz et al. 2018: 417;Suddaby 2006). Through attending to our participants' perceptions, language, and experiences, our study sheds light on their views and practices of network leadership, and provides new theoretical insights on (non)leadership phenomena in collaborative interorganizational networks and on shared leadership development. We developed our findings through analytic induction by iteratively shifting between data-inspired induction and theory-inspired deduction for imaginative practice-oriented theorizing (Suddaby 2006;Charmaz 2014). In doing so, we rely on informed grounded theory, which is neither abstract (or naive) empiricism nor pure (subjectivist) relativism. Hence, grounded theory ''is not an excuse to ignore the literature'' (Suddaby 2006: 634;Charmaz et al. 2018: 419;Charmaz 2014). In line with this understanding, we applied ''constant comparison'' and ''theoretical sampling'', which are considered core principles of grounded theorizing (Suddaby 2006;Charmaz 2014;Glaser and Strauss 1967). Constant comparison fundamentally implies an iterative cyclical research process in which the researcher shifts between collecting and analyzing data (see below for more details). Theoretical sampling means making decisions on what data to collect next on the basis of themes and concepts that emerged with theoretical relevance for the theory that is being constructed (cf. Charmaz 2014;Suddaby 2006: 634).

Title: Sport Administrators' Perspectives on Advancing Safe Sport
Snippet: Constant comparisons and memo-writing are often relied upon when analysing data in grounded theory research. Charmaz (2006) defined the constant comparative method as: 

A method of analysis that generates successively more abstract concepts and theories through inductive processes of comparing data with data, data with category, category with category, and category with concept. Comparisons then constitute each stage of analytic development (p. 187). 

At each stage of analysis, constant comparisons were made as part of the coding process. A CGTM includes two main phases of coding-initial and focused-followed by a process of theoretical coding (Charmaz, 2006). During initial coding, we thoroughly read through the transcript data line-by-line (Jones et al., 2014) and answered the questions, "What are these data a study of?" and "What do the data suggest?" (Charmaz, 2006, p. 47); answering these questions assisted in the naming of initial codes. Next, we engaged in a process of focused coding, which permitted us to develop more selective, directed and abstract codes (Charmaz, 2006). In this stage of analysis, focused codes develop into theoretically rich and integrative categories (Jones et al., 2014). 

The final theoretical codes depict potential relationships between categories of codes developed through focused coding (Charmaz, 2006). The grounded theory that emerges from the data is founded on the formation of the integrative theoretical codes (Charmaz, 2006;Jones et al., 2014). 

Lastly, analysis occurred through a process of memo-writing, ". . . the fundamental process of researcher/data engagement that results in a "grounded" theory" (Lempert, 2007, p. 245). snippet.text: Interpretive grounded theory (Charmaz 2014;Suddaby 2006;Glaser and Strauss 1967) is usually contrasted with a positivist approach of qualitative research (cf. e.g. Gephart 2004 on the distinction between positivist and non-positivist/interpretive qualitative research). From an interpretive perspective, ''truth'' is considered as provisional, and social life as well as leadership as processual (Charmaz 2014: 17;Charmaz et al. 2018;cf. Endres and Weibler 2017: 217f.;cf. Astley 1985;Morgan and Smircich 1980). Hence, research ''seeks interpretive understanding rather than a variable analysis that produces abstract generalizations'' (Charmaz et al. 2018: 417;Suddaby 2006). Through attending to our participants' perceptions, language, and experiences, our study sheds light on their views and practices of network leadership, and provides new theoretical insights on (non)leadership phenomena in collaborative interorganizational networks and on shared leadership development. We developed our findings through analytic induction by iteratively shifting between data-inspired induction and theory-inspired deduction for imaginative practice-oriented theorizing (Suddaby 2006;Charmaz 2014). In doing so, we rely on informed grounded theory, which is neither abstract (or naive) empiricism nor pure (subjectivist) relativism. Hence, grounded theory ''is not an excuse to ignore the literature'' (Suddaby 2006: 634;Charmaz et al. 2018: 419;Charmaz 2014). In line with this understanding, we applied ''constant comparison'' and ''theoretical sampling'', which are considered core principles of grounded theorizing (Suddaby 2006;Charmaz 2014;Glaser and Strauss 1967). Constant comparison fundamentally implies an iterative cyclical research process in which the researcher shifts between collecting and analyzing data (see below for more details). Theoretical sampling means making decisions on what data to collect next on the basis of themes and concepts that emerged with theoretical relevance for the theory that is being constructed (cf. Charmaz 2014;Suddaby 2006: 634).

Constant comparisons and memo-writing are often relied upon when analysing data in grounded theory research. Charmaz (2006) defined the constant comparative method as: 

A method of analysis that generates successively more abstract concepts and theories through inductive processes of comparing data with data, data with category, category with category, and category with concept. Comparisons then constitute each stage of analytic development (p. 187). 

At each stage of analysis, constant comparisons were made as part of the coding process. A CGTM includes two main phases of coding-initial and focused-followed by a process of theoretical coding (Charmaz, 2006). During initial coding, we thoroughly read through the transcript data line-by-line (Jones et al., 2014) and answered the questions, "What are these data a study of?" and "What do the data suggest?" (Charmaz, 2006, p. 47); answering these questions assisted in the naming of initial codes. Next, we engaged in a process of focused coding, which permitted us to develop more selective, directed and abstract codes (Charmaz, 2006). In this stage of analysis, focused codes develop into theoretically rich and integrative categories (Jones et al., 2014). 

The final theoretical codes depict potential relationships between categories of codes developed through focused coding (Charmaz, 2006). The grounded theory that emerges from the data is founded on the formation of the integrative theoretical codes (Charmaz, 2006;Jones et al., 2014). 

Lastly, analysis occurred through a process of memo-writing, ". . . the fundamental process of researcher/data engagement that results in a "grounded" theory" (Lempert, 2007, p. 245). Memos were written with an analytical, rather than a descriptive, mindset (Jones et al., 2014). As the analysis progressed, literary resources were examined so that the theoretical underpinnings of other research could aid in identifying patterns within our dataset (Lempert, 2007).
